items.readable_text:
Content:
We'll explore some properties of parallelograms in this lesson. Let's begin by stating the definition of a parallelogram.

Content:
> A parallelogram is a quadrilateral where the opposite sides are parallel.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ac3c2d89635dbc0d71c0bf368986bbd6]

Content:
It's possible to prove the following property.

Content:
> In a parallelogram, the opposite sides are congruent.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a12cf95048a7f12ad650f9b2bf7bb8fb]

Content:
The fact that the opposite sides are congruent is a consequence of the definition of a parallelogram, not part of the definition itself. We'll learn how to prove this in future lessons.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In any parallelogram, the opposite sides are congruent. So, we have

[MATH: AB|= CD; 2x + 5|= 15; 2x|= 10; x|= 5,]

and therefore,

[MATH: AD|= x + 5; = 5 + 5; = 10.]

Using again the fact that the opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent, we get

[MATH: BC|= AD = 10.]

items.title: Finding Diagonal Lengths of Parallelograms

key_prerequisites.name: Segment Bisectors and the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem

sections.normalized_html: For the parallelogram [MATH: ABCD] shown above, find the length of the diagonal [MATH: \overline{BD}.]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/4dc5c48ad9b487a9b5f520726b084ee4]

For the parallelogram [MATH: ABCD] shown above, find the length of the diagonal [MATH: \overline{BD}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. That is, they intersect at their respective midpoints. In our case, this means that

[MATH: \qquad BO = DO \quad] and [MATH: \quad CO = AO.]

Now, since [MATH: CO = AO,] we have

[MATH: AO|= CO; 3x + 9|= 27; 3x|= 27 − 9; 3x|= 18; x|= 6.]

As a result,

[MATH: BO|= 7x − 5; = 7 ⋅ 6 − 5; = 42 − 5; = 37.]

Finally, since [MATH: BO = DO,] we obtain

[MATH: BD|= BO + DO; = BO + BO; = 2BO; = 2 ⋅ 37; = 74.]

key_prerequisites.name: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution

sections.normalized_html: The diagonals [MATH: \overline{AC}] and [MATH: \overline{BD}] of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] above intersect at the point [MATH: O.] If [MATH: AO = 4x+3,] [MATH: BO = 5-x,] [MATH: CO = y+2,] and [MATH: DO=y-1,] find the values ​​of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] such that [MATH: ABCD] is a parallelogram.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/faa4ea19a876aaa518bf090f6dc0f933]

The diagonals [MATH: \overline{AC}] and [MATH: \overline{BD}] of the quadrilateral [MATH: ABCD] above intersect at the point [MATH: O.] If [MATH: AO = 4x+3,] [MATH: BO = 5-x,] [MATH: CO = y+2,] and [MATH: DO=y-1,] find the values ​​of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] such that [MATH: ABCD] is a parallelogram.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Thus, [MATH: ABCD] is a parallelogram if [MATH: AO=CO] and [MATH: BO=DO.]

  • Using the first equality, we have [MATH: AO|= CO; 4x + 3|= y + 2; y|= 4x + 1.]

  • Using the second equality, we get [MATH: BO|= DO; 5 − x|= y − 1; x|= 6 − y.]

Substituting [MATH: y = 4x+1] from the first equation into the above, we have

[MATH: x|= 6 − y; x|= 6 − (4x + 1); x|= 5 − 4x; 5x|= 5; x|= 1.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: x] back into the first equation, we get

[MATH: y|= 4x + 1; = 4 ⋅ 1 + 1; = 4 + 1; = 5.]

Therefore, [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: y=5.]

[MATH: y|= 4x + 1; = 4 ⋅ 1 + 1; = 4 + 1; = 5.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We'll explore some properties of parallelograms in this lesson. Let's begin by stating the definition of a parallelogram.

Content:
> A parallelogram is a quadrilateral where the opposite sides are parallel.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ac3c2d89635dbc0d71c0bf368986bbd6]

Content:
It's possible to prove the following property.

Content:
> In a parallelogram, the opposite sides are congruent.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a12cf95048a7f12ad650f9b2bf7bb8fb]

Content:
The fact that the opposite sides are congruent is a consequence of the definition of a parallelogram, not part of the definition itself. We'll learn how to prove this in future lessons.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
Consider the parallelogram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/00191dcaf9989d9effbc88214fefe144]

Content:
What are the measures of the sides [MATH: \overline{CD}] and [MATH: \overline{BC}?]

Content:
- Since the sides [MATH: AB] and [MATH: CD] are opposite, we have [MATH: CD = AB = 3.]
- Since the sides [MATH: AD] and [MATH: BC] are opposite, we have [MATH: BC = AD = 2.]

Content:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f510f6cc434bad2586831c89e22ff428]

Item 3 — Example: Finding Side Lengths of Parallelograms

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In any parallelogram, the opposite sides are congruent. So, we have

[MATH: AB|= CD; 2x + 5|= 15; 2x|= 10; x|= 5,]

and therefore,

[MATH: AD|= x + 5; = 5 + 5; = 10.]

Using again the fact that the opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent, we get

[MATH: BC|= AD = 10.]

[MATH: m∠B|= 180^{∘} − m∠A; = 180^{∘} − 70^{∘}; = 110^{∘}.]

Since [MATH: \angle{A}] and [MATH: \angle{D}] are adjacent angles of the parallelogram [MATH: ABCD,] we obtain

Item 13 — Tutorial: Diagonal Lengths

Content:
All parallelograms have the following property.

Content:
> The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

Content:
In other words, the first diagonal of a parallelogram bisects the second, and the second diagonal bisects the first, as shown below.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. That is, they intersect at their respective midpoints. In our case, this means that

[MATH: \qquad BO = DO \quad] and [MATH: \quad CO = AO.]

Now, since [MATH: CO = AO,] we have

[MATH: AO|= CO; 3x + 9|= 27; 3x|= 27 − 9; 3x|= 18; x|= 6.]

As a result,

[MATH: BO|= 7x − 5; = 7 ⋅ 6 − 5; = 42 − 5; = 37.]

Finally, since [MATH: BO = DO,] we obtain

[MATH: BD|= BO + DO; = BO + BO; = 2BO; = 2 ⋅ 37; = 74.]

Item 17 — Tutorial: The Diagonal Criterion

Content:
We've already seen that if a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, its diagonals bisect each other.

Content:
The converse of this statement is also true.

Content:
> If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then it is a parallelogram.

Content:
For example, consider the quadrilateral shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a74638c70edfbc2620d696bada2df202]

Content:
Note that

Content:
- the diagonal [MATH: \overline{BD}] bisects the diagonal [MATH: \overline{AC},] and
- the diagonal [MATH: \overline{AC}] bisects the diagonal [MATH: \overline{BD}.]

Content:
Therefore, this quadrilateral must be a parallelogram!

---

- Using the first equality, we have
[MATH: AO|= CO; 4x + 3|= y + 2; y|= 4x + 1.]
- Using the second equality, we get
[MATH: BO|= DO; 5 − x|= y − 1; x|= 6 − y.]

Substituting [MATH: y = 4x+1] from the first equation into the above, we have

[MATH: x|= 6 − y; x|= 6 − (4x + 1); x|= 5 − 4x; 5x|= 5; x|= 1.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: x] back into the first equation, we get

[MATH: y|= 4x + 1; = 4 ⋅ 1 + 1; = 4 + 1; = 5.]

Therefore, [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: y=5.]
